plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four sub-panels (a through d) showing the different matrix representations used to encode a graph for graph neural networks. Panel a) depicts a 6-node undirected graph with nodes labeled 1 through 6, connected by edges whose identities are marked by the pair of endpoint node labels (e.g., ‘1\3’, ‘1\4’, ‘2\3’, ‘3\4’, ‘3\6’, ‘4\5’, ‘5\6’). Panel b) shows the adjacency matrix A (N × N), a square binary matrix encoding which pairs of nodes are connected by edges. Panel c) shows the node feature matrix X (D × N), in which each column stores the D-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the N nodes. Panel d) shows the edge feature matrix E (Dᴷ × E), in which each column stores the Dᴷ-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the E edges, with edges ordered to match the labeled pairs in panel a). Labels for each matrix include its name, symbol, and dimensions. This figure introduces the three standard data structures—adjacency matrix, node feature matrix, and edge feature matrix—that together fully represent a graph with node and edge attributes in a deep learning context.

interactions.label: Representation view
interactions.teaches: The same graph can be viewed as a visual network, a connectivity matrix, a node-attribute table, or an edge-attribute table
A node corresponds to one row and one column in the adjacency matrix and to one column in the node feature matrix
An edge corresponds to a pair of connected nodes in the graph, two symmetric adjacency entries, and one column in the edge feature matrix

demo_steps.title: Start with the graph
demo_steps.narration: Panel a shows the graph as circles and connecting lines. The small stacked cells near nodes and edges indicate that both nodes and edges can carry feature vectors.

demo_steps.title: Connectivity becomes A
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the adjacency matrix: every filled cell marks a pair of nodes connected by an edge. Because the graph is undirected, the matrix is symmetric.

demo_steps.title: Nodes become columns of X
demo_steps.narration: Switch to node data: each node label now names a column of X, and each column stores that node's feature vector.

demo_steps.title: Edges become columns of E
demo_steps.narration: Switch to edge data: each column of E is indexed by an endpoint pair such as 1–3 or 4–5, so edge attributes are stored separately from node attributes.

demo_steps.title: Link the representations
demo_steps.narration: Return to all panels and click a node or edge. The highlights show how a single graph object maps to the corresponding matrix rows, columns, and feature vectors.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The graph picture and the matrices are not separate objects: nodes, edges, connectivity, and attributes are the same information organized into different arrays.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a wide four-panel layout matching the source: graph on the left, adjacency matrix in the middle, node data in the upper right, and edge data in the lower right. Draw graph edges in blue-gray and nodes as white circles with brown outlines and black labels. Place node 3 near the lower-left center as a hub connected to nodes 1, 2, 4, and 6; node 4 connects onward to 5, and 5 connects to 6. Use brown/peach color palettes for node features and teal palettes for edge features. The adjacency matrix should be a 6×6 square grid with dark outlines and blue-gray filled cells for the seven undirected edges in both symmetric positions. When a node is clicked, highlight that node in panel a, its full row and column in A, and its column in X. When an edge is clicked, thicken or glow the graph edge and its two endpoint nodes, highlight the two symmetric cells in A, and highlight the matching column in E according to the edge order (1,3), (1,4), (2,3), (3,4), (3,6), (4,5), (5,6).
